subject: astronomy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the celestial equator?
options: The projection of the Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere
The apparent yearly path of the Sun
A line joining the two celestial poles
The circle marking the observer's horizon
questions.explain: The celestial equator is the great circle formed by extending the Earth's equatorial plane out onto the celestial sphere.

questions.q: In what units is right ascension usually measured?
questions.explain: Right ascension is measured in hours (0h to 24h) eastward around the celestial equator from the First Point of Aries.

questions.q: In what units is declination measured?
questions.explain: Declination is an angle in degrees, positive north of the celestial equator and negative south of it, ranging from +90 to -90.

questions.q: The declination of a star tells you its angular distance from which reference?
options: North or south of the celestial equator
West of the north celestial pole
questions.explain: Declination is the celestial equivalent of latitude, measuring how far north or south of the celestial equator an object lies.

questions.q: An observer stands at latitude 52 degrees N. What is the approximate altitude of Polaris above their horizon?
questions.explain: The altitude of the north celestial pole (marked closely by Polaris) equals the observer's latitude.

questions.q: What does the term 'zenith' describe?
options: The point on the celestial sphere directly above the observer
The point where the Sun rises
The southern point of the horizon
The star nearest the celestial pole
questions.explain: The zenith is the point directly overhead, at an altitude of 90 degrees for that observer.

questions.q: Why does the Sun appear to trace the ecliptic against the background stars over a year?
options: Because the Earth orbits the Sun
Because the Sun orbits the Earth once a year
Because the celestial sphere spins daily
questions.explain: The ecliptic is the Sun's apparent annual path, which results from the Earth's orbital motion around the Sun.

questions.q: What is a circumpolar star?
options: A star that never sets below the observer's horizon
A star that is only visible at the equator
A star that rises and sets each day
A star found only in the southern hemisphere
questions.explain: Circumpolar stars stay above the horizon at all times, appearing to circle the celestial pole as the Earth rotates.

questions.q: For an observer at latitude L, a star is circumpolar if its declination is greater than which value?
questions.explain: A star never sets if its declination exceeds (90 degrees - latitude), keeping it above the horizon throughout the night.

questions.q: For an observer at latitude 54 degrees N, which star declination would be circumpolar?
questions.explain: The star must have a declination greater than (90 - 54) = 36 degrees, so +50 degrees qualifies.

questions.q: The Plough is a well-known asterism found within which constellation?
questions.explain: The Plough is an asterism (a recognisable pattern) forming part of the larger constellation Ursa Major.

questions.q: Which two 'pointer' stars in the Plough are used to locate Polaris?
questions.explain: A line drawn through the pointer stars Merak and Dubhe leads the eye to Polaris, the pole star.

questions.q: Why do circumpolar stars appear to trace circles around the celestial pole during the night?
options: Because the Earth rotates on its axis
Because the stars physically orbit Polaris
questions.explain: The Earth's daily rotation makes the sky appear to turn, so circumpolar stars circle the fixed celestial pole.

questions.q: Under a clear, dark sky, roughly what is the faintest apparent magnitude visible to the unaided human eye?
questions.explain: In good dark-sky conditions the naked eye can detect stars down to about magnitude +6.

questions.q: On the apparent magnitude scale, how are brighter objects represented?
questions.explain: The scale runs in reverse, so the brighter an object appears, the lower or more negative its magnitude.

questions.q: What is the main effect of light pollution on naked-eye observing?
options: Fewer stars are visible because the sky background is brighter
Stars appear to move faster across the sky
questions.explain: Light pollution raises the brightness of the sky background, drowning out fainter stars so fewer can be seen.

questions.q: Approximately how long does it take for the eyes to become fully dark-adapted?
questions.explain: Full dark adaptation, which greatly improves sensitivity to faint objects, takes roughly 20 to 30 minutes.

questions.q: What is 'averted vision' and why is it useful?
options: Looking slightly to one side of a faint object to use the more sensitive edge of the retina
Closing one eye to reduce glare
Staring directly at an object for a long time
Using a red torch to read charts
questions.explain: Looking slightly off-centre places the image on rod-rich peripheral retina, which is more sensitive to faint light.

questions.q: A difference of 5 magnitudes corresponds to a brightness ratio of approximately what?
questions.explain: By definition a difference of 5 magnitudes equals a brightness factor of exactly 100.

questions.q: For an observer at latitude 51 degrees N, at what altitude does the celestial equator cross the meridian due south?
questions.explain: The celestial equator meets the southern meridian at an altitude of (90 - latitude) = 39 degrees.
